item.title: Fazl clarifies he criticised policies, not institutions after ministers allege he sought 'share' in KP governance
item.description:
Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman on Saturday clarified that his party’s remarks regarding the country’s security situation were directed at policies, not institutions, and termed the allegations levelled against him by federal ministers as character assassination.

A day earlier, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, without naming anyone, had claimed that a “head of a party” was “extremely upset” about not being appointed the governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The remarks came after Fazl accused the Centre of depriving the provinces of their rights and raised doubts over its reasoning behind imposing governor’s rule that there was a lack of cooperation on counterterrorism.

Earlier on Saturday, State Minister for Interior Tallal Chaudhry also rebuked the JUI-F chief for reportedly seeking his “share” in KP’s governance following the imposition of governor’s rule and an emergency in the province. Other federal ministers have also taken exception to Fazl’s remarks.

Addressing a press conference in Lahore on Saturday, Fazl stressed that his party’s criticism was directed at policies, not institutions, and was intended to bring about corrective action rather than undermine the sacrifices made in the fight against terrorism.

The senior politician called for an in-camera session of Parliament to review the country’s security situation and formulate a consensus-based policy to combat terrorism.

“Our only question is why the country has failed to eliminate terrorism. Let us sit together and find out why. Parliament is the most appropriate forum to discuss the issue and make decisions. Instead of ridiculing politicians, the government should take them on board in this fight so that we can move forward together,” he said.

“If Parliament is supreme, why are decisions taken in Rawalpindi while Parliament is simply told to follow them?” he remarked. “The issue is that this government is powerless. Decisions are taken somewhere else, and it implements them obediently,” he alleged.

The JUI-F maintained that Parliament should review the security situation and that the nation should be taken into confidence. If the public was expected to support the fight against terrorism and those engaged in it, he argued, the government should explain its decisions rather than impose “unilateral measures”.

Fazl reiterated his objection to the imposition of emergency rule in KP or any other part of the country. Recalling his family’s opposition to emergency rule in Balochistan during the 1970s, he said his father had resigned when the government of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto imposed it in the province.

He described the recurrence of such measures as unfortunate, pointing out that the PP had repeatedly been associated with their imposition.

Questioning the rationale behind the emergency, governor’s rule and deployment of troops in KP, Fazl asked why the province should face such treatment when Balochistan was also grappling with the same level of terrorist violence, if not more.

The JUI-F chief urged the government to develop a shared national narrative and a consensus-based counterterrorism strategy instead of questioning his party’s position.

He went on to ask why the government engaged in negotiations with the PTI, which had been in power in KP, if the party was accused of supporting terrorists. “On top of it, both (the PTI and the government) say that they had reached a consensus on all points.”

Fazl then highlighted that around 250 of his party workers had lost their lives in terrorist violence, arguing that their sacrifices should not be ridiculed or overlooked. “How can a party whose members have laid their lives be accused of supporting terrorists?” he asked.

He also questioned why he was being singled out for criticism when political leaders, including former prime minister Nawaz Sharif, had at various times disagreed with the military leadership.

Ministers assail Fazl

Earlier on Saturday, addressing the media in Jaranwala, Chaudhry said, “I am upset. We did not expect Maulana sahib […] to consider this as spoils of war and seek his share in the absence of a PTI government in the province.”

He emphasised that the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP was not a political move aimed at strengthening the PML-N’s presence in the province by dismissing the PTI-led government.

“This was an administrative setup,” he said, adding that it had been formed with a “one-point agenda: combating terrorism”, rather than with an intention of establishing a political setup.

“This is not spoils of war,” he reiterated, adding that the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP was an “immensely responsible” decision taken after every other option had been considered.

“I am unable to understand why Maulana sahab says that he was forced to accept defeat [in elections],” he said, arguing that Fazl’s party had been defeated by the PTI in KP and the Pashtunkhwa Milli Awami Party in Balochistan.

Chaudhry said the JUI-F was worthy of respect only if it stood by Pakistan’s interests.

The state minister also rejected the impression that the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule was aimed at taking control of KP’s natural resources.

He also criticised Fazl for bringing up the 1971 separation of East Pakistan — now Bangladesh — from Pakistan in his recent statements.

“You bring up 1971 after losing the 2024 elections,” Chaudhry said.

“This KP setup is not about distributing shares, forming coalitions and governments, or engaging in politics,” he stressed, clarifying that only one member of the KP Advisory Council has a political background, as she represents the families of martyrs.

Chaudhry again offered to implement the National Action Plan and combat terrorism jointly with all stakeholders. “Politics is possible only where there is peace,” he said.

At the outset of his address, Chaudhry alleged that there must be “a relationship or a mutual interest arrangement between the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and the PTI”.

“Since 2015, no PTI leader, gathering or member has been targeted by terrorists,” Chaudhry said. “On the other hand, over the past 11 years, no political or religious party, security force, public office, funeral or wedding has been spared terrorist attacks.”

He said the federal government had exhausted all avenues to bring together stakeholders and urge them to condemn terrorism by naming those involved, whether the TTP, the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), or groups funded by India or Afghanistan.

The state minister claimed that in 2013, when the government decided to hold talks with the TTP and representatives were proposed by both sides, the TTP had nominated PTI founder Imran Khan to its committee.

He also alleged that the PTI founder had allowed the TTP to open offices in Peshawar.

During his address, Chaudhry also criticised the PTI, showing a press release issued by the TTP that condemned the dismissal of the party’s government.

Meanwhile, speaking at a press conference in Sialkot, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif criticised the JUI-F chief for constantly “targeting” the country’s security forces.

He declared that the sacrifices made by the security forces, officers, and the public in the fight against terrorism were “matchless”.

The defence minister referred to Fazl’s accusations that the emergency and governor’s rule were imposed to capture KP’s mineral resources, saying that he had shared a full list of people who had the mining contracts in KP.

Asif maintained that the whole PTI and opposition leadership was engaged by the government before the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule.

“But it was fruitless,” he said.

“The situation will improve in KP […] parliament can roll back the decision of imposing the emergency only if the improvement of the situation in the province is guaranteed,” the defence minister said.

He said that some individuals in KP were expecting to get a share in the administrative changes in the province.

“We will ensure free and fair elections. Whenever the time comes, everybody can take part in it,” he said.

Fazl’s remarks also prompted a response from KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi, who has now been tasked with running the province under governor’s rule.

Kundi, referring to the JUI-F chief, asked whether “your land in the land belonging to martyrs in DI Khan is halal”.

“What you get is halal, what the other gets is haram,” he remarked.

The governor reaffirmed that the new KP administration would continue to function properly.

‘Extremely upset’

Fazl, who was involved in reducing tensions between the Centre and the KP government, has been critical of the federal government over the imposition of governor’s rule in KP. He also accused the Centre of reneging on its commitments amid his efforts to mediate between the two parties.

Addressing a rally in Multan on Thursday, Fazl further recalled that his party had expressed reservations over the merger of tribal areas into KP after the 25th Constitutional Amendment in 2018.

“We were not against the merger, but we said that it was an issue of the political future of the people of tribal areas,” he said, alleging that the people of those areas were not consulted on the merger.

He alleged governor’s rule was not imposed in Balochistan because the province’s chief minister “praises you”.

The next day, during an interaction with journalists, the interior minister said, “The head of a party is extremely upset over being denied a role in the new setup in KP and not getting the governorship.”

This politician, Naqvi alleged, had remained “dependent on the establishment for decades to advance his political career”.

“These are the same politicians who remained in politics for decades with the support of the establishment, and this politician even relied on the establishment to arrange air tickets for the members of his party,” he further alleged.

He said such politicians had little justification for criticising others now, particularly after having benefitted from the same system they currently denounced.

The same day, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz also railed against Fazl in a post on X.

She said it was not expected of a senior politician such as him to support those who facilitate terrorism — an apparent reference to the PTI, which the Centre accuses of backing terrorism.

She also criticised Fazl for his remarks about Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, seemingly referring to his comments during the Multan address about the centralisation of power.

The Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP on Oct 11, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism.

The move has drawn criticism from the opposition, including Fazl, as well as Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Raja Nasir Abbas of the Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan.

In the days preceding the imposition of governor’s rule in KP, political tensions between the Centre and the opposition — including the PTI which was in power in KP — had remained high since jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s party announced a protest march to Islamabad to demand his release.

Intense negotiations between the two sides a week before the imposition of governor’s rule had failed to yield any results, while Fazl was cast as the man who could defuse heightening tensions between the Centre and the PTI. Both sides had held separate meetings with Fazl, reportedly for his intervention to help break the deadlock in the negotiations.

item.title: India's 'cockroach' movement founder released from police custody
item.description:
India’s Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke was released from detention on Saturday, a day after he was detained during a police crackdown on protests against the election authority.

Dipke, 31, was detained on Friday in New Delhi as he headed to join a rally that the CJP protest movement had called in the capital’s central Connaught Place district. He was arrested to prevent a breach of the peace, broadcasters NDTV and ​India Today reported.

He walked out of a police station on Saturday afternoon, waving to the media and giving a thumbs up as he was driven away, an AFP photographer saw.

“Abhijeet Dipke released,” CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh said on social media.

Opposition parties and CJP activists have defied a security crackdown, rallying to demand the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar after accusing the poll body of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.

More than 130 million voters were deleted ​during the revision. The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol. The BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.

Student activist Neha ​Bora, a prominent face of the protests, who was also detained on Friday as she ​tried to reach central Delhi with dozens of supporters, was released earlier on Saturday as well.

“Please, spare the people of India. ‌Impeach ⁠Gyanesh Kumar and halt SIR (special intensive revision), so that the ordinary citizens of this country can breathe a sigh of relief, feel at ease, and have their voting rights ensured,” Bora told ANI news agency after she was released.

Two other senior CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, were arrested on Oct 14 after entering Jantar Mantar, a decades-old protest site that police have declared off-limits for demonstrations. They remain in custody.

Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.

Rights groups and critics, however, say Modi’s government has eroded democratic freedoms during more than a decade in power, citing pressure on journalists, civil society groups and political opponents — allegations the government rejects.

A weeks-long sit-in by supporters of the movement earlier this year forced then-education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation over ​exam paper leaks.

BRTA makes front number plates mandatory for motorcycles
item.description:
The Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA) has made it mandatory for motorcycles to display number plates at the front, setting November 15 as the deadline for installation.
Motorcycle owners must install manually made number plates at the front in addition to the digital plates already required at the rear. Those who fail to comply by the deadline will face legal action, it said.
In an urgent public notice issued on Friday, the BRTA said the Road Transport Act, 2018 and the Road Transport Rules, 2022 already require motorcycles to have retro-reflective number plates equipped with Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) tags at the rear.
To strengthen traffic management and surveillance, the authority has now decided to require registration numbers to be displayed at the front as well.
The front number plates must be made of stainless steel or aluminium, with a white background and black Bengali letters and numerals. No designs or decorative elements will be allowed.
The notice also specifies different dimensions for scooters and other motorcycles.
For scooters, the plate must be 200mm long and 100mm wide, while for other motorcycles, it must be 285mm long and 50mm wide. In both cases, the letters and numerals must be at least 20mm high.
The BRTA has urged motorcycle owners to install the plates in accordance with the prescribed specifications before the deadline.

item.title: Muhammad Yunus receives ‘Hillary Rodham Clinton Award’
item.description:
Former chief adviser to the interim government of Bangladesh and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus has received the prestigious ‘Hillary Rodham Clinton Award’.

Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton presented the award to Grameen Bank founder Muhammad Yunus at a grand ceremony held at Georgetown University in Washington on Thursday.

Around 400 guests, including ambassadors from about 25 countries, entrepreneurs, teachers and researchers, attended the ceremony at the university’s Gaston Hall.

As soon as Muhammad Yunus’s name was announced, the audience rose to its feet and gave him a prolonged standing ovation.

A total of four people, including Muhammad Yunus, received the honour this year. The other recipients were India’s Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA) director Reema Nanavaty, Tory Burch Foundation founder and fashion designer Tory Burch and board chair of Jordan’s Microfund for Women Muna Sukhtian.

Muna also received the special ‘Georgetown Ambassadors Award’.

Praising Muhammad Yunus at the ceremony, Hillary Clinton said, “I have personally seen the work of Grameen Bank and seen how women have become self-reliant and ensured their own security and empowerment.”

Describing the work as unprecedented, she said, “It is not only the women of Bangladesh but Dr Yunus has spread his work across the world.”

In his acceptance speech, Muhammad Yunus referred to the completion of 50 years of his work and said, “This is a recognition of 50 years of our work. The event you have organised here will convey an important message to Bangladesh and inspire Grameen families.”

Highlighting Grameen Bank’s role in poverty alleviation and women’s empowerment, he said, “Through microcredit, we have helped people living in extreme poverty stand on their own feet.”

“We have focused on women so that they can use their own strengths, take responsibility for themselves and improve their families’ financial conditions,” he added.

“Today, we no longer see poor women sitting quietly and shyly. Instead, we see confident women who speak up about their problems and needs. These women run their own bank, and they are the owners of Grameen Bank,” Yunus added.

Referring to the children of borrowers who are now seeking employment, Yunus said they had been told to repeat the message, “We are not job seekers, we are job creators.”

Speaking about the concept of social business, he said its purpose was not to generate personal profit but to solve problems.

“Social business funds are supporting the establishment of hospitals, healthcare centres and eye hospitals in different parts of the country. Any surplus generated by these institutions is being reinvested in healthcare,” he added.

Criticising the current education system, Muhammad Yunus said it had been wrongly structured because it prepared young people to seek jobs.

“The purpose of education should be to develop people’s creativity and entrepreneurial spirit and the education system should focus on creating entrepreneurs,”

Muhammad Yunus also revealed that Grameen University would be launched by the end of this year to help achieve that goal, according to a press release.

He said Grameen University could take the lead in building a “Three Zeros” world.

“The university will seek to teach students to become entrepreneurs instead of merely pursuing certificates. It will provide the necessary support, including financing, to help them start businesses,” he added.

He hoped that the initiative would mark a new beginning in the field of education.

item.title: Question paper reaches 2 NBR employees before dawn, spreads with answers within hours
item.description:
At 4:43 am, a blurry photograph of the question paper arrived on the mobile phone of Nur Mohammad, an office assistant at the National Board of Revenue (NBR). Nearly an hour and a half later, at around 6:15 am, Jahangir, a computer operator at the same organisation, received a clearer photograph of the same question paper.

An answer sheet was then prepared and circulated among other members of the network. Through them, it reached prospective candidates and people seeking to buy the leaked questions.

The Special Response Battalion (SRB) said it had pieced together this sequence by examining mobile phone conversations and data retrieved from the phones of those arrested in connection with the leak of the recruitment examination questions for assistant youth development officer posts at the Department of Youth Development.

Over the past three days, the force arrested seven people in raids in Dhaka and elsewhere in the country. Besides NBR employees, those arrested include staff members of the Department of Environment and the Ministry of Defence.

Based on information provided by the arrestees, the force seized 116 stamp papers each costs Tk 100, four Tk 50 stamp papers, a set of question papers, 19 pages of admission cards for various examinations, 10 certificates of different categories, another 15 certificates of various types, 48 pages of bank cheques from different banks, a cheque book from one bank, six national identity cards and Tk 4,000 in cash.

The arrestees are Nur Mohammad, 30, an office assistant at the NBR; Jahangir, 38, an NBR computer operator; SM Imdadul Islam, 35, an NBR computer operator; Asadul Islam, 33, an office assistant at the Ministry of Defence; Md Rubel Islam, 33, a data entry operator at the Department of Environment; and two other members of the network, Mofizul Islam, 23, and Md Hasinur Rahman alias Sujon.

Lieutenant Colonel Faizul Arefin, commander of SRB-3, disclosed the information at a press conference at the SRB media centre in Karwan Bazar, Dhaka, on Friday afternoon.

Last Saturday, candidates took to the streets and blocked roads in different parts of Dhaka to protest the question paper leak in the Department of Youth Development recruitment examination.

The Ministry of Youth and Sports formed a five-member committee the same day to investigate the allegations, appointing an additional secretary to head it. The committee has yet to submit its report. Meanwhile, the recruitment examination was held again today.

Shadow investigation launched after question paper leak

Lieutenant Colonel Faizul Arefin, commander of SRB-3, said the recruitment test for 242 vacant assistant youth development officer posts at the Department of Youth Development had been scheduled for 10 October. A total of 319,000 jobseekers had applied.

The examination was scheduled to begin at 11:00 am that day, but the authorities postponed it after confirming the question paper leak at 10:03 am.

The SRB launched a shadow investigation following the incident. On 11 October, the Department of Youth Development filed a case with Motijheel police station. The SRB intelligence team began investigating to identify the possible source of the question paper, those supplying it, intermediaries distributing it and its buyers.

The force subsequently found evidence pointing to the involvement of an organised network. Acting on that information, it arrested seven people in raids in Dhaka and elsewhere on 14, 15 and 16 October.

Raids began in Motijheel before spreading to other areas

At the press conference, the SRB said preliminary inquiries had pointed to the involvement of Rubel Islam, a data entry operator at the Department of Environment. He was arrested along with two others in Motijheel, Dhaka, while money was allegedly being transferred in connection with an admission-related racket.

Mofizul, one of those arrested, is a jobseeker. After being defrauded of Tk 1.7 million by a member of a racket, he joined the network in the hope of making more money.

Information provided by the arrestees and an analysis of their mobile phone conversations led investigators to other members of the network. SM Imdadul Islam, a computer operator at the NBR, was arrested in the Uttarkhan area, while Asadul Islam, an office assistant at the Ministry of Defence, was arrested in Mirpur-10, Dhaka.

Later, based on mobile phone chat records, SRB-4 arrested NBR office assistant Nur Mohammad in Savar on Thursday. On Friday, evidence and information obtained from him led to the arrest of Jahangir, a computer operator at the same organisation, in Mohammadpur.

From question paper to answer sheet, then distribution

Lieutenant Colonel Faizul Arefin said an examination of messages exchanged on the arrested individuals’ mobile phones had revealed a sequence of events showing how the question paper was obtained and distributed.

According to the investigation, at around 4:43 am on 10 October, NBR office assistant Nur Mohammad received a blurry photograph of the question paper from an unidentified source. At around 6:15 am, Jahangir sent him a clearer photograph of the paper.

Nur Mohammad then prepared answers to the questions and sent them to Jahangir and his colleague Imdadul Islam. Preliminary findings suggest that the information was subsequently passed on to the network members’ own candidates and those involved in distributing the leaked questions.

Investigators found indications of the involvement of Asadul Islam, Rubel Islam, Mofizul Islam and Hasinur Rahman Sujon.

The network used fake identities on WhatsApp to communicate and conduct transactions. Its members sold the leaked questions and answer sheets to candidates they knew for Tk 800,000 to Tk 1 million.

During questioning, the suspects did not disclose how many people had bought the questions from them. They said they had been involved in leaking question papers for various recruitment examinations.

According to their statements, they charged Tk 800,000 to Tk 1 million for question papers for third-class recruitment examinations and Tk 1.5 million to Tk 2 million for second-class recruitment examinations.

During questioning, Nur Mohammad and Jahangir failed to give satisfactory answers about who had supplied them with the question paper for the assistant youth development officer recruitment examination.

Asked whether anyone at the Department of Youth Development had been involved in the leak, SRB official Faizul Arefin said the matter could be confirmed after the investigation was completed.

item.title: TIB: State reform held hostage by power politics a year after July Charter signing
item.description:
Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) has said the opportunity to establish an accountable system of government and reform the state created by the July mass uprising has been held hostage by power politics and a bureaucratic vicious cycle, a year after the July National Charter was signed.
TIB Executive Director Iftekharuzzaman made the remarks in a statement on Friday, expressing concern over the direction of state reforms and the government’s decisions on constitutional changes, judicial independence and accountability.
According to Iftekharuzzaman, the interim government failed to make the most of the opportunity created by the July mass uprising because of a lack of strategic planning and political courage, alongside compromises with bureaucratic resistance.
Following the 13th parliamentary election, the legal, institutional and bureaucratic ecosystem has continued to be shaped by power politics, he said. The reform process has therefore remained constrained by political interests rather than being directed towards establishing an accountable system of government.
The decisions taken by the government have raised questions about its commitment to the reform agenda, particularly where changes depend on political consensus and the willingness of those in power to accept greater accountability.
The ruling alliance’s position on constitutional amendments and state reform, alongside opposition parties’ pursuit of partisan gains, has complicated the implementation of the reform agenda.
The ruling party had presented a 31-point agenda and pledged in its election manifesto to implement state reforms and the July National Charter “to the letter”.
However, ruling party members of parliament refused to take the oath as members of the proposed Constitutional Reform Council despite having supported the referendum, raising questions about the implementation of the reform commitments.
The role of the Constitutional Amendment Committee has also become part of the wider debate over the future of the reform process and the extent to which political parties are prepared to honour their commitments.
The interim government issued 133 ordinances, many of which the current government has since enacted. However, decisions to repeal or suspend accountability-related ordinances while enacting measures that make executive powers less accountable have raised concerns about the direction of reform.
The slogan “Now it is our turn” has also drawn attention in the context of questions about whether the political transition is delivering institutional change or reproducing existing patterns of power.
Among the measures repealed were the Supreme Court Secretariat (Amendment) Ordinance and the Supreme Court Judges Appointment Ordinance.
Instead of proceeding with the amended bill concerning the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC), the government returned to the ACC Act 2004.
The National Human Rights Commission Ordinance was also repealed and replaced with a new law. The ordinance on enforced disappearances was repealed, while legislation was introduced that, according to the criticism raised over the changes, protects the agencies concerned.
Although the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) was said to have been abolished, the force was further empowered under a new name.
The absence of an independent police commission has also raised concerns about accountability in law enforcement. Similarly, there has been no clear indication that asset declarations required within three months of taking office are being implemented.
The decisions affecting the judiciary, law enforcement agencies, the ACC and the National Human Rights Commission have raised broader concerns about the independence of institutions responsible for ensuring accountability.
Iftekharuzzaman’s concerns centre on the risk that institutions meant to provide oversight could become partisan, weakening their ability to hold the executive branch accountable.
The developments have also raised questions about whether the reform process is addressing the institutional weaknesses associated with authoritarian rule or allowing similar patterns to persist under a new political arrangement.
The concerns extend beyond individual ordinances or institutions to the wider system of checks and balances, including the independence of the judiciary and the effectiveness of mechanisms designed to investigate abuses and prevent the misuse of state power.
TIB has called on political parties to uphold the consensus reached on the July National Charter and follow through on their commitments to state reform.
The organisation has stressed the importance of implementing the agreed reforms to strengthen democracy, improve governance and ensure social justice.
It has also warned against allowing partisan interests and bureaucratic resistance to undermine the opportunity for meaningful institutional change created by the July mass uprising.
TIB’s call comes amid concerns that failure to honour the reform commitments could leave the country vulnerable to a return to authoritarian rule.

item.title: 107 flights to Saudi Arabia cancelled, 16,620 passengers stranded
item.description:
A total of 107 flights from Dhaka to Riyadh and Dammam airports were cancelled from October 10 to Friday due to the closure of the 2 airports, leaving 16,620 passengers stranded.
Kawser Mahmud, assistant director of the public relations department of the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB), confirmed the information on Friday afternoon.
He said 44 of the cancelled flights were direct flights, including 17 operated by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, 10 by US-Bangla Airlines, 10 by Saudia and 7 by Riyadh Air.
Another 63 transit flights were cancelled. These included 22 operated by IndiGo, 7 by SalamAir, 1 by EgyptAir, 14 by Emirates, 9 by Qatar Airways, 6 by flydubai and 4 by Air India.
Mahmud said flight cancellations would continue until the situation returned to normal and the airports resumed normal operations.

item.title: Dengue: Four more die, 1,181 hospitalized in 24 hours
item.description:
Four people died of dengue, and 1,181 were hospitalized after being infected with dengue in the last 24 hours till 8am on Friday, according to a regular report of Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
With four deaths in the past 24 hours, the death toll from the disease stood at 335 this year.
Of the newly hospitalized dengue patients, 410 were in Dhaka Division, 92 in Mymensingh Division, 242 in Chittagong Division, 140 in Khulna Division, 99 in Rajshahi, 71 in Rangpur Division and 127 in Barisal Division.
According to the report, a total of 108,440 dengue patients have so far been hospitalized across the country this year.
However, in the last 24 hours, 1,179 patients recovered and were discharged from hospitals.
So far, 102,210 dengue patients have recovered and returned home after receiving treatment in hospitals.
A total of 102,861 people were infected with dengue, and 413 people died from the disease last year.

item.title: Titumir: WB, IMF see Family, Farmers’ Card helping reduce poverty
item.description:
The World Bank (WB) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) believe the government's Family Card, Farmers' Card and other social protection programs can help ease people's economic hardship and reduce poverty amid prolonged inflation and the ongoing Middle East crisis.
The initiatives are expected to help lift people who have fallen below the poverty line out of poverty while preventing vulnerable households from slipping into poverty, said Prime Minister's Adviser on Finance and Planning Prof Dr Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir.
He made the remarks on Friday while briefing journalists on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group in Bangkok.
Earlier in the morning, a Bangladesh delegation led by Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury held meetings with officials of the World Bank, IMF, Standard Chartered Bank and Bank of America.
Dr Titumir said prolonged inflation and the Middle East crisis had increased the cost of living, particularly for low-income and working-class people.
Rising fuel and electricity prices could also affect various sectors of the economy, he added.
"The government is taking necessary measures to address these pressures," he said, adding that it is trying to minimize the additional burden on ordinary people when adjusting fuel prices.
Referring to recent World Bank reports and assessments by international organizations, the adviser said prolonged inflation had increased the risk of more people falling below the poverty line.
According to World Bank estimates cited by him, around eight million people in Bangladesh had fallen below the poverty line due to prolonged inflation in the past.
He said the Family Card and Farmers' Card programs were expected to play an important role in addressing the situation.
One of the major weaknesses of previous social safety net programs was the inaccurate selection of beneficiaries, Dr Titumir said.
Many eligible people were excluded, while some ineligible individuals were included in the lists, he added.
To address the problem, the government is emphasizing the use of digital public infrastructure to ensure that assistance reaches the actual beneficiaries, he said.
Citing assessments by independent research organizations, the adviser said effective implementation of the Family Card program could reduce poverty by around 5%.
He said the programs were not merely aspirational plans but were included in the Prime Minister's election manifesto and the government's five-year economic strategy.
Dr Titumir said strict monetary policy alone would not be sufficient to control inflation, stressing the need for reforms in revenue collection and the financial sector.
The government aims to increase revenue mobilization and move away from tax evasion, tax fraud and a culture of patronage, he said, adding that revenue collection had already shown positive changes following the reform initiatives.
Revenue growth stood at around 3% in the last fiscal year. However, after the present government assumed office, revenue growth rose to 12-13% during the period from mid-February to June 30, he said.
The credibility of the government's reform agenda would be demonstrated through tangible results, the adviser added.
Regarding the IMF's economic projections, he said forecasts should be interpreted in light of their underlying assumptions and the prevailing circumstances.
"The projections should also be viewed against the possible consequences of failing to implement reforms," he said, adding that the government wanted to overcome doubts among international partners stemming from unfulfilled commitments under the previous Sheikh Hasina administration.
Highlighting the need to restore discipline in the banking sector and rebuild depositors' confidence, Dr Titumir said financial losses equivalent to around US$40 billion had come to the fore following widespread irregularities and the siphoning of funds in the past.
The government was working to restore confidence in the banking system, he said.
He noted progress in rebuilding depositors' confidence in Sammilito Islami Bank, saying customers had been able to withdraw money according to their needs since September 1.
Many depositors were also placing money in the bank while withdrawing funds, which he described as an indication of improving confidence.
The decline in Treasury bond interest rates was another positive sign of changes in the financial sector, he added.
Dr Titumir said the Middle East crisis had increased import costs for fuel, liquefied natural gas (LNG) and fertilizer.
However, calculating the additional import expenditure alone would not fully capture the crisis's impact on the economy, he said.
The government's decision to refrain from increasing diesel prices to reduce pressure on farmers should also be taken into account, he added.
Although Bangladesh had no role in creating the crisis, the government was working to address its consequences out of its responsibility to the people, he said.
The adviser said the prime minister had adopted a strategy to transform Bangladesh into a manufacturing hub and an export gateway to accelerate economic recovery, create jobs and increase production and exports.
The government's objectives include boosting domestic revenue, restoring confidence in the banking sector and reducing economic pressure on households to create a pathway towards sustainable development, he added.
The 2026 Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group and the IMF are being held in Bangkok, Thailand from October 12 to 18.
The meetings at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center have brought together finance ministers, central bank governors, policymakers, development partners and private-sector representatives from across the world.
Global economic challenges, development financing, poverty reduction, job creation, investment expansion and financial-sector reforms are among the key issues under discussion.
For Bangladesh, the meetings provide an important opportunity to advance discussions with international partners on economic reforms, development financing and programs aligned with the country's priorities.

item.title: National Parliament committee proposes annual assessments to enhance education quality
item.description:
The Standing Committee on the Ministry of Education of the 13th National Parliament has recommended introducing an annual assessment system aligned with international standards to improve quality of education and move beyond artificial competition over pass rates.
At its first meeting held at the National Parliament Building on September 10, the committee proposed a series of measures to ensure transparency in education spending, tackle irregularities and corruption, investigate declining secondary-level enrolment, strengthen teacher training and expand technical education.
Chairman of the committee and Member of Parliament Md Salim Bhuiyan told Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha (BSS) at the Secretariat yesterday that the previous government had focused on numerical indicators and pass rates rather than genuine educational quality.
“Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's government does not believe in this artificial competition. We want to ensure genuine quality in education in the country,” he said.
He stressed the need for annual assessments, a modern curriculum and evaluations of learning outcomes at three- or six-month intervals to bring students in line with international standards.
Further recommendations and details of the government's education roadmap will be presented at a press conference, he added.
Committee member Reza Kibria also emphasized setting specific annual benchmarks to ensure Bangladeshi students perform competitively in international assessments, particularly in mathematics and science.
Members proposed a long-term national education vision, modelled on Malaysia, to prevent frequent changes to education policies, curricula and textbooks following changes in government.
According to the meeting minutes, the government has proposed a budget of Tk57,301.68 crore for the Secondary and Higher Education Division in the 2026-27 fiscal year, 42.7% higher than the previous revised budget.
The initiatives discussed included distributing laptops to approximately 40,000 students who achieved a Golden GPA in 2026 and bringing seven million female students under a Tk4,000 crore scholarship program to promote girls’ education and reduce dropout rates.
The committee also acknowledged the transfer of outstanding dues to the bank accounts of around 70,000 retired teachers and employees through the Electronic Fund Transfer (EFT) and iBAS systems.
In the initial phase, each teacher is receiving an average of Tk5 lakh.
The committee thanked Prime Minister Tarique Rahman for providing Tk2,000 crore in special assistance to address the crisis involving teachers' welfare and retirement benefits.
It recommended expediting MPO enlistment for eligible non-MPO institutions and long-serving teachers, reducing bureaucratic delays and investigating the significant decline in secondary-level enrolment.
Technical and Madrasah Education Division Secretary (routine charge) Shamsur Rahman Khan informed the meeting that technical education enrolment reached 19.16% in 2025, with a target of 30% by 2030.
Other decisions included field visits by committee members to inspect educational institutions, mandatory attendance of education board heads and National University representatives at future meetings, and faster settlement of outstanding allowances, subject to budget availability.
Educationists have welcomed the proposals, particularly the shift towards measurable learning outcomes and international standards, as potentially significant steps towards improving education quality.

item.title: Speakers: Climate-vulnerable countries must not be pushed into debt trap
item.description:
Climate-vulnerable countries must not be pushed into a new debt trap in the name of climate adaptation, speakers said at a human chain program in Mongla on Friday.
They said developed countries and corporations continue to profit from fossil fuel-dependent economies, while farmers, workers and climate-vulnerable nations bear the brunt of cyclones, droughts, river erosion and crop losses.
The speakers called for a just transition to green energy, environmental protection, climate justice and public ownership of resources.
The human chain program was held at Mithekhali Bazar in Mongla, coinciding with the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank in Bangkok, Thailand, scheduled for October 12-18. The event focused on the question of whose interests the global economy serves.
Dharitri Rakkhay Amra, Pashur River Waterkeeper, Udayan Youth Sangha, and Waterkeepers Bangladesh jointly organised the program.
Nur Alam Sheikh, a central leader of DHORA and Pashur River Waterkeeper, presided over the event. Speakers included Prof Nazrul Islam, labour leader Nazmul Haque, DHORA leader Molla Al Mamun, farmer leader Asaduzzaman Tito, SM Jane Alam Babu of Udayan Youth Sangha, youth leaders Sheikh Sifatullah Shuvo and Arafat Durjoy, and Mehedi Hasan of Waterkeepers Bangladesh.
Nazmul Haque said developing countries were struggling to repay foreign loans and interest while meeting essential spending needs in education, healthcare, agriculture and social protection. High interest rates, rising energy prices and climate-related disasters were further aggravating the crisis, he said.
“If people’s fundamental rights are curtailed to repay loans, who is development for?” he asked, stressing that public needs must take precedence over lenders’ conditions.
In his address, Nur Alam Sheikh said communities affected by climate change should receive fair compensation, not loans, for the losses and damage they suffer. “We must build a world for people, not for profit,” he said, calling for adequate climate financing and investment in renewable energy.
He also urged the government to ensure that food was treated as a fundamental human right rather than a source of corporate profit, promote environmentally friendly agriculture and ensure a just transition to green energy.
“Financing renewable energy is financing climate action,” he said, calling for an immediate shift to renewable energy.

item.title: European leaders rally around Zelensky as Trump ties slump
item.description:
European leaders on Friday rallied around Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky as Kyiv’s ties with US President Donald Trump have nosedived and worries grow that US leader is increasingly siding with Russia.
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since last week, when Trump eased sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel onto global markets.
Zelensky infuriated Trump further by ordering Ukraine’s forces to restart strikes on Russian oil refineries in defiance of Washington’s demands.
Meanwhile anger in Ukraine has been heightened by disruptions to a critical US-provided satellite system that has hampered its military’s ability to counter Russia’s intense bombardments ahead of the harsh winter months.
“This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” European Council chief Antonio Costa said, standing alongside Zelensky at an EU summit in Brussels. “Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.”
The Ukrainian president welcomed the backing of “real leaders” in Europe and said there were no signals that Moscow is ready “to end this war.”
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that “the situation in Ukraine is currently truly dire, with numerous Russian attacks and a tense relationship between Ukraine and the US.”
“It is crucial that we, as Europe, demonstrate our unconditional support for them today -- and explore what additional steps we can take,” he said.
Zelensky has had to endure a rollercoaster relationship with Trump since the mercurial US leader returned to office last year vowing to cut Washington’s support for Kyiv.
Trump on Thursday branded renewed Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure a “disgrace” and said Kyiv was driving up global energy prices.
“I think I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin,” the US leader said in an interview with Newsmax.
The Kremlin has sought to capitalize on the latest breakdown between Kyiv and Washington, blaming Ukraine for derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes on refineries.
Ukraine meanwhile has accused the Trump administration of essentially helping Moscow during the latest falling out as the bad blood appears to have hit Ukraine’s ability to defend itself.
Despite the tensions, European leaders are hoping that Ukraine can weather the storm and patch up ties as there is little substitute for key US satellite capabilities.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in (the) short term Europe can’t replace this capability,” EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas said.
Ukraine uses the Starshield system from Elon Musk’s SpaceX for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones.
It is separate from SpaceX’s parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Ukraine also uses but not for offensive operations.
Tech billionaire Musk, who has also called for Zelensky to be replaced as leader, said his company was not behind any disruption to the system.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he added, referring to Trump.
While the main focus for European leaders will be on overcoming the latest crisis with Washington, they will also focus on how to bolster Ukraine’s air defenses and cover Ukraine’s dire budgetary situation.
“We have to prepare for the winter. It’s not only energy, it’s also air defense and fundings,” Zelensky said.
EU leaders are set to open discussions about how to keep Ukraine afloat next year in the face of a growing realization that funds will run dry.
The EU has in place a $101-billion loan for Kyiv that was set to help cover funding to the end of 2027.
But the Ukrainian authorities have warned they will need tens of billions more as Russia’s strikes have battered the country’s economy.
The talks around the new funding have reignited calls for the European Union to tap around 200 billion euros in frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine.
“The frozen assets are there. That’s what should be used for supporting Ukraine,” said Latvian premier Andris Kulbergs.
But there seems little momentum on that front as Belgium, where most of the funds are held, remains opposed.

item.title: Eighteen passenger railway coaches arrive from India
item.description:
Eighteen broad-gauge passenger railway coaches imported from India entered Bangladesh through the Darshana-Jaynagar border in Chuadanga at 3pm on Friday.
After completing customs formalities at Darshana, the coaches will be taken to Bangladesh Railway’s workshop in Saidpur for inspection before being added to the railway fleet.
The coaches began their journey from Kapurthala in India’s Punjab state on Monday, October 12. They remained at Ranaghat Station in Kolkata before departing on Friday afternoon.
After completing formalities at India’s Gede border checkpoint, the coaches entered Bangladesh through the Darshana-Jaynagar border. Officials of Bangladesh Railway’s Pakshey division subsequently took charge of the shipment.
The coaches have been painted red and green. The shipment includes 3 air-conditioned chair coaches, air-conditioned berth coaches, 4 luggage vans and 11 Shovon chair coaches.
In May 2024, the Bangladesh government signed an agreement with India’s RITES Limited under a project to purchase broad-gauge railway coaches.
The coaches were procured from RITES Limited in India. A total of 200 coaches will be collected from India in several phases and added to Bangladesh Railway’s fleet.
Robiul Islam, divisional mechanical engineer of Bangladesh Railway’s Pakshey division, said 18 broad-gauge passenger coaches had entered Bangladesh from India on Friday.
He said the coaches belonged to different categories and that the government had taken the initiative to improve the quality of passenger services.

item.title: The U.S. eliminated measles 26 years ago. Now it could lose that status in a matter of weeks
item.description:
The U.S. declared measles eliminated in 2000—but it could soon lose that status, depending on the conclusions of a meeting of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) next month.

Measles cases in the United States are rising; there could be twice as many cases in 2026 as in 2025. The measles tracker run by John Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health counted 4,267 cases as of October 15. The total for last year was 2,286. 

Pennsylvania has accounted for more than a quarter of the 2026 cases, with 1,136. South Carolina and Utah had the next-highest statewide counts, at 671 and 527, respectively; but almost every state has seen at least one case this year. 

MEASLES’ ELIMINATION, AND RETURN

In the decades after the first measles vaccine became available in 1963, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) set a goal to eliminate the disease.

The CDC defined the elimination of a disease as a reduction to zero within a “defined geographical area as a result of deliberate efforts.” That finally happened almost 40 years later, in 2000, when a period with no continuous spread of measles lasted for more than a year.

Now, measles has been spreading within the U.S. for almost two years.

“That the U.S. will likely lose elimination status is one of many indicators of our eroding public health system,” Amria Roess, a professor of global health and epidemiology at George Mason University and former CDC officer, said in a measles tip sheet the university published this week.

“We now have so many unvaccinated individuals that we are seeing widespread local transmission of measles,” she said.

Fully 97% of this year’s measles cases were in people who are either unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown, according to the Johns Hopkins tracker. Experts estimate that more than 95% of a population needs immunity to measles to prevent large outbreaks, KFF Health News writes, but only 10 states had reported those coverage levels in 2024-25.

A POSTPONED MEETING

A meeting of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) to review the U.S.’s ​measles elimination status was set to take place in April, but was rescheduled for November, after the midterm elections. There has been some ambiguity about the reasons behind the decision.

PAHO, which is the arm of the World Health Organization for the Americas, stated that the change aimed “to simplify and harmonize the process” based on the commission’s meeting schedule, and also allowed the U.S. more time to conduct data analysis. A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Andrew Nixon, said in March that U.S. health officials had asked for the delay. But in response to a question from Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester, Democrat of Delaware, during a Senate hearing the following month, the HHS secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., denied that the agency had made the request. 

The CDC “appreciates PAHO’s agreement” to reschedule, which provided additional time to assess the measles outbreaks, another HHS spokesperson, Grace Davis Jamison, said in an email. She did not clarify what role HHS had in the decision-making process. 

She added that the agency “has mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks across the country,” referring to a recent move to provide $100 million in additional funding to states for measles preparedness and response efforts. 

“Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles,” she said.

Kennedy has promoted antivaccine sentiments and applied them to federal health policy.

President Donald Trump’s orders around vaccine scheduling have elicited backlash from Democrats, and the antivaccine sentiments of the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement are frequently criticized and debunked by experts. Only 38% of voters approve of the Trump administration’s handling of vaccine policy, according to a KFF poll from May. 

PAHO’s annual meeting will take place November 10-13, days after the midterms.

There, the commission will examine “the re-establishment of endemic measles transmission,” the organization said in an October 14 press release. This occurs, the organization said, when evidence indicates “that a chain of transmission involving a viral strain with an identical genotype and lineage has continued uninterrupted for 12 months or longer” within a given country or area.

item.title: Fed chair Warsh says price stability is key but deflects on rate signals
item.description:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said Friday he won’t prejudge what the U.S. central bank will do about interest rates at its upcoming meetings in October and December.

The Fed increased its key interest rate by a quarter-point to about 3.9% in September, its first increase in three years, and stubbornly elevated U.S. inflation will likely lead it to hike that rate again in coming months to slow spending and help cool price pressures.

But Warsh offered no fresh signals during a “fireside chat” with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok.

“At the Federal Reserve, we made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago,” Warsh said. “I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.”

The Fed’s September rate hike defied U.S. President Donald Trump’s repeated calls for the Fed to cut rates. The president criticized the Fed’s rate-setting committee, though he still expressed support for Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year.

The global surge in prices is a key concern of central bankers and financial leaders meeting in Bangkok.

According to minutes released from the most recent meeting, most Fed officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year. That would raise borrowing costs for mortgages, car loans, and credit cards over time.

Warsh said the surge in investment driven by the craze for artificial intelligence is one of the factors behind higher inflation and the Fed’s task force on issues related to AI will meet Nov. 16.

“I’d say the advent of this new technology is probably the most consequential change to the U.S. and the global economy in my lifetime to this point,” he said.

Unlike military conflict and other shocks that are driving prices higher, Warsh said he believes AI will bring “huge benefit” to the world economy in time.

For Fed economists who struggle to foresee the future using data that lags behind today’s realities, AI could prove a vital tool, he said.

“We torture data with old fashioned models to try to find out what’s underlying inflation trends. Not so long from now, it won’t be torture. We will have access at the fingertips of central banks to all the information in the world, and we’ll be able to use new analytical tools to distill that data,” he said.

—Elaine Kurtenbach, AP business writer

AP Economics Writer Christopher Rugaber and AP journalist Haruka Nuga contributed to this story.

item.title: Why the Paramount‑Warner merger threatens democracy
item.description:
Media critic Ben Bagdikian warned in 2004 that five corporations had accumulated “more communications power than was exercised by any despot or dictatorship in history.” More than 20 years later, a major media merger is bringing his warning back into focus.

Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery in October 2026 created a new company, Skydance Corporation. It now owns CNN and CBS News, Warner Bros. and Paramount Pictures, HBO and Paramount+, along with a sprawling collection of cable networks, live sports and entertainment franchises. The deal is valued at about US$110 billion including debt, and Skydance expects to cut at least $6 billion in costs within three years.

A coalition of 12 states sued to stop the merger on antitrust grounds, arguing that it would reduce competition in movies and television. The eventual settlement required a multiyear movie production and theatrical release guarantee and an editorial independence board for CNN and CBS News. CNN chief Mark Thompson and CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss remain in charge, but both ultimately report to Skydance CEO David Ellison.

Lawmakers have already raised concerns about possible political influence over CBS News, though Ellison has denied interfering with coverage. President Donald Trump, a frequent CNN critic, publicly praised the merger.

As a scholar who studies the role of media in democratic societies, I believe that size and ownership matter. Whoever owns the media chooses its leaders, approves its budgets and decides where to cut $6 billion. The same market pressures pushing media companies toward greater scale and efficiency can undermine the independent reporting and diversity of voices that democracy depends on.

When media are more than ordinary products

Since broadcasting began, American media policy has wrestled with how to support the information needs of a democracy.

As my work on the origins of media systems shows, the United States built a largely private, commercial broadcasting system while Britain created the publicly funded BBC. Behind those choices were different ideas about whether broadcasting should operate primarily as a business or carry broader obligations to the public.

The market view became increasingly dominant in the U.S. In 1981, the Ronald Reagan-era chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, Mark Fowler, famously described television as “a toaster with pictures.” He argued that broadcasters should largely respond to audiences through ordinary market forces.

But as media scholar Robert McChesney argued in 1999, concentrated commercial media had become a “significant antidemocratic force.” What makes money for a media company and what citizens need from a media system are not always the same thing.

We’ve seen this film before.

Local television stations acquired by Sinclair Broadcast Group in 2017 shifted coverage away from local politics and toward national political stories. As research shows, communities that lose local media coverage can see less competition and participation in elections.

Mergers, however, make sense in the logic of the market. Warner and Paramount must compete with Netflix, YouTube, Amazon, Apple and other companies with enormous resources and global reach.

But having fewer competitors can also mean there’s less pressure to improve quality or hold down prices. And the efficiencies of media consolidation often come from producing less original content with fewer people.

The new gatekeepers

Concerns about media power are hardly new.

The 1947 Hutchins Commission on Freedom of the Press warned about control of mass communication becoming concentrated in fewer hands, and it encouraged greater social responsibility. For decades, the FCC placed limits on broadcast ownership to support competition and diversity.

Digital media seemed to blow open the gates that limited participation, but a new class of gatekeepers arrived. While Bagdikian mainly worried about companies that owned newspapers, TV networks and movie studios, today’s media power lies in the hands of platforms, streamers and tech giants.

Social and video platforms have overtaken TV and news sites as the most common way people access news in dozens of countries studied in 2026 by the Reuters Institute. News organizations may still produce a story, but Google, YouTube, Facebook, TikTok and artificial intelligence can determine whether anyone sees it.

For social platforms, attention is the commodity. Likes, shares, comments, clicks and watch time help determine what gets promoted. And more time on the platform means more opportunities to sell ads.

It’s now well documented that social media feeds ranked for that kind of engagement expose people to more toxic political content and moral outrage than chronological feeds. They also increase perceptions of hostility between political groups.

Americans certainly consume enough media, with combined use at more than 13 hours a day.

Yet Americans do not seem especially well-informed or confident about the information they receive. Only 33% say they trust mass media to report the news fully and fairly, compared with 68% when Gallup first asked in 1972, and about half say they have difficulty determining what is true in the news. More than a third cannot name all three branches of the federal government.

Media concentration did not cause all of these problems. But decades of greater media abundance have not solved problems of knowledge, misinformation or trust.

Who produces the information democracy needs?

Democracy assumes that citizens will have enough information to make choices and hold powerful institutions accountable. But markets provide no guarantee that anyone will produce it.

As media scholar C. Edwin Baker explained in 2009, journalism creates benefits that extend far beyond the person who buys a newspaper or subscription. A monthslong investigation of corruption might benefit an entire city, including thousands of people who never pay for the reporting. But the media organization still has to cover the cost.

That’s why restoring journalism requires public and nonprofit alternatives to combat market failures, as media scholar Victor Pickard has laid out.

Other democracies already rely more heavily on a mix of commercial and public media. Research in 2009 comparing the U.S. with Britain, Denmark and Finland found that stronger public service outlets carried more public affairs and international news and were associated with greater political knowledge.

This doesn’t have to be a partisan issue. Regardless of who is in power, citizens benefit from vibrant journalism with the resources and independence to investigate government, business and other powerful institutions.

Media literacy can help citizens understand why the system works this way. As I argue in my 2019 book, News Literacy and Democracy, examining media means understanding the structures and institutions behind it—who owns them, how they make money and what pressures shape what gets produced.

But there are limits to what we can ask individual news consumers to fix.

People can learn to check sources and spot misinformation, but they can’t change market forces. The Paramount-Warner merger makes sense according to the logic of the market, and I believe that’s the problem. The same pressures that push media companies toward greater scale and lower costs can work against creating the media environment that democracy needs to thrive.

Seth Ashley is an associate professor of journalism and media communication at Colorado State University.

item.title: ​​Libya: Racism and ‘resettlement’ conspiracies fuel fear among Tripoli’s migrants
item.description:
​​Libya: Racism and ‘resettlement’ conspiracies fuel fear among Tripoli’s migrants

Submitted by Driss Rejichi on Thu, 10/15/2026 - 13:08
A surge in anti‑migrant protest is reshaping life for Sub‑Saharan people already living in precarious conditions
Libyans outside the International Organization for Migration in Tripoli demand action against irregular migrants and refugees, on 16 June 2026 (Mahmud Turkia/AFP)
Off

1 October was supposed to be the “deadline” for foreign migrants in Tripoli. In the weeks leading up to it, dozens of groups and pages on social media urged Libyans to take to the streets in openly xenophobic protests.

Featuring racist slurs and depictions of Sub-Saharan, Arab and Asian migrants, the widely shared Facebook posts were intimidating.

The migrant rights group Refugees in Libya even reported receiving a handwritten threat targeting “black people”, delivered with a bullet, days before the planned protest.

Eventually, the demonstrations barely materialised, overshadowed by a large teachers’ strike over unpaid salaries directed at Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, head of the Government of National Unity (GNU), which rules the west of the divided country.

Still, dozens of protesters took to the streets in Tripoli on 2 and 9 October, rallying in Martyrs’ Square and chanting “Libya for Libyans” and “No to resettlement”.

Similar demonstrations have taken place several times a month in central Tripoli since April, steadily fuelling hostility towards migrants.

With nearly 700,000 Sub-Saharan Africans living in the Tripoli area, including some 335,000 Sudanese refugees fleeing the war, the Libyan capital has become a major hub for migrants seeking to reach Europe.

Between January and August, Libya was the departure point for around 80 percent of the 19,000 migrants who reached Italy through the Mediterranean. More than 90 percent of departures occurred from western Libya, particularly the coastline between Tripoli and Zuwara, long known as a major launch point for boats.

Attacks on migrant aid agencies

Already exposed to smuggling networks, arbitrary detention, kidnapping, torture and slavery – “systematic human rights violations and abuses”, according to the UN – as well as violent interception at sea, migrants now face growing threats in their homes and workplaces.

“I feel that Libyans are increasingly allowed to do whatever they want to us, without obligation to abide by the law,” Albert G, a 37-year-old Sierra Leonean living in eastern Tripoli, told Middle East Eye.

“Not only will torture and imprisonment continue to be a reality for migrants, which is already a well-known problem, but it also adds more common difficulties when there is no way for us to enter the public places or look for work to survive.”

‘I feel that Libyans are increasingly allowed to do whatever they want to us, without obligation to abide by the law’

– Albert, Sierra Leonean migrant

Albert says hostility began rising with the first protests in spring and became genuinely frightening at the start of summer.

In June, large crowds of Libyans protested for the first time against what they called a “resettlement plan”, allegedly orchestrated by the United Nations to prevent migrants from leaving the country.

Despite firm denials from the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), hundreds of protesters blocked the UNHCR headquarters in Tripoli on 4 June, accusing international agencies of trying to alter Libya’s demographics.

The protests were accompanied by anti‑migrant violence and waves of arrests of Sub-Saharans by the police and armed factions aligned with the interior ministry across several western Libyan cities, prompting many Sub‑Saharan people to remain indoors for days.

Although the unrest subsided during the summer, small gatherings and sporadic incidents continued.

On 7 September, tensions escalated when a group of Libyans stormed an IOM Migrants' Response Centre in western Tripoli. No casualties were reported, but the attack deeply unsettled the Sub‑Saharan community.

“If the authorities can allow an IOM camp to be attacked, many lives will be impacted because there will be no safe place for migrants,” Albert said.

Authorities accused of ‘complacency’

Following the incident, the GNU stated that “the right to peaceful protest can never justify assault, vandalism or threats to life”, warning that perpetrators could face legal action.

Asked by MEE about steps taken since the attack, the interior ministry failed to respond.

Meanwhile, popular Facebook and X pages created in spring remain active, spreading hate speech and promoting calls for mobilisation. Groups such as “Libyan News – No to the Resettlement In Libya” (76,000 members) and “The Tripoli Activists Movement” (39,000 members) continue to share hateful content targeting migrants daily.

Libya: Video reveals young Ethiopian woman being tortured for ransom 
Read More »

The degree of coordination behind the movement and its origin remain unclear. A BBC investigation in August found that the June protests were fuelled by online rumours.

On the ground, public figures such as lawyer Thuraya al-Tuwaibi and journalist Salma al‑Shaab have repeatedly led protests – which they call "peaceful" – reinforcing their momentum.

“These campaigns are still ongoing, even though they are based on false and misleading information,” Ahmed Hamza, a Libyan human rights activist, told MEE.

“The actions of those advocating for or coordinating this criminal movement constitute criminal acts punishable under the Libyan Penal Code,” he added.

Hamza pointed to “a state of complacency, complicity, and suspicious silence from the interior ministry and other authorities”.

Migrants echo this sentiment, saying that while the GNU allows them to live and work in Libya – and sometimes even employs them – it has never guaranteed their safety in Tripoli.

‘I have never felt safe in Libya’

Kingsley (pseudonym), a Cameroonian refugee who has lived in Tripoli for four years, told MEE he has “never felt safe in Libya”.

Arrested twice by security forces in 2024 and 2025, the young man says he was released only after paying money to what he describes as his “kidnappers”. Beyond criminal gangs, armed groups affiliated with state institutions have been repeatedly accused of holding civilians to ransom.

“Now, I see the vast majority of Libyans as a threat,” Kingsley said.

‘Now, I see the vast majority of Libyans as a threat’

– Kingsley, Cameroonian refugee

While Sub‑Saharan Africans remain the main targets of online hate campaigns, some posts also target Palestinian, Syrian and Bangladeshi communities – particularly present in eastern Libya but increasingly visible in Tripoli.

Migrants also report more frequent violations of their rights and disrespect from locals amid the hostile climate, even when incidents are not directly linked to the anti‑resettlement movement.

“Last week, I worked at a construction site for two days and received no money. I had to go home on an empty stomach,” Albert said.

New protest dates have not been announced yet, but tensions around the anti‑resettlement movement continue to simmer, raising concerns that the situation could worsen.

“Authorities must assume their responsibilities. Matters could escalate and get out of control,” Hamza warned.

So far, the hostile climate has not prompted large numbers of migrants to leave Tripoli, but some are considering it. The IOM operates voluntary return programmes that assisted around 16,000 migrants in 2025, while the Libyan authorities deported more than 37,000 last year.

“Even if the situation is terrible there too, I would rather be in Tunisia, or Algeria,” Albert said. “I don’t know what the coming months have in store for us here.”

item.title: France faces day of cost-of-living protests
item.description:
French authorities detained dozens on Saturday at the start of nationwide protests against the cost of living, in what is likely to be a key indicator of the social climate heading toward elections to replace President Emmanuel Macron.
With just months to go before the two-round elections in April and May to choose Macron’s successor, the demonstrations follow weeks of high-school student blockades demanding better learning conditions.
These have at times turned into violent clashes, and sparked criticism from rights groups that the police have used disproportionate force in response.
The main Paris demonstration was to kick off at 2pm (1200 GMT) at the Republique square.
The country’s Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against Macron’s government over planned fuel tax hikes, has called Saturday’s “yellow and youth” demonstrations.
It has appealed to teachers and students, workers, pensioners and farmers to take part in the protests on the first day of half-term holidays.
The protests geared up with a handful of gatherings nationwide on Saturday morning, AFP reporters said.
In the western city of Rennes, around 20 people set up a barricade using trash bins and large pallets on the outskirts of a shopping mall.
Christophe, a 47-year-old carpenter and former Yellow Vest protester who did not give his surname, said he was indignant after seeing what he viewed as police brutality against teenagers in recent weeks.
“We’ve reached the point where the repression is targeting our own children,” he told AFP.
In the southern city of Marseille, some protesters attacked a police building, an AFP photographer saw.
Demonstrators clashed with police -- who responded with tear gas -- and briefly blocked a main road with rubbish bins and scooters before officers cleared it.
“We’re here to protest the deplorable resources allocated to education and against police brutality,” said Aude, a masked student who did not give her surname.
In Paris, where the authorities have banned protests around government buildings, the Champs-Elysees shopping avenue and train stations, police detained around 60 people on Saturday morning.
Police officers asked passersby for ID outside the Saint-Lazare station, AFP reporters said.
Protesters in balaclavas in the morning threw projectiles and broke windows at the headquarters of the right-leaning television broadcaster CNews.
“It’s not just a Yellow Vest movement, it’s not just a student movement, it’s all the people who are rising up and that’s why those in power are afraid,” said Benjamin Ball, an activist working on a website for the demonstrations.
More than 600 demonstrations were planned across France, according to the website set up by organizers.
Around 45 percent of French people are worried about the cost of living and inflation, according to a survey of 2,000 people published earlier this month.
Macron on Friday evening called “for calm and respect.” In Brussels for European Union talks, he added the right to protest went hand in hand with “respect for people and property.”
The unrest has been seized upon by France’s far-left and far-right parties.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, has backed the student protests and marched in one demonstration Tuesday supporting them.
Marine Le Pen, who leads in opinion polls for the presidential race, has positioned her National Rally party on the side of the police.
